title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{264272}
Let $N\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$. Then $N$ is a symmetric complex matrix if and only if $\boldsymbol{j}N$ is a skew-Hermitian quaternion matrix.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that for $N\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$, $\boldsymbol{j}N=\overline{N}\boldsymbol{j}$. The fact that $\boldsymbol{j}N$ is skew-Hermitian is equivalent to $N^{\ast}\boldsymbol{j}=\boldsymbol{j}N(=\overline{N}\boldsymbol{j})$. Then, $\boldsymbol{j}N$ is skew-Hermitian if and only if
$N^{T}=N$, i.e., $N$ is symmetric complex.
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{264281}
If $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is symmetric, then there exists a unitary matrix $U\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ and a nonnegative diagonal matrix $\Upsilon$ such that
$$
U^{T}AU=\Upsilon.
$$
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{12}
For any complex matrix $C$, the equality $C\boldsymbol{j}=\boldsymbol{j}\overline{C}$ holds.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{1}
Assume $p,q\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $p\sim q$ if and only if $|p|=|q|$ and $p_{0}=q_{0}$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{2}
Let $p=a\boldsymbol{i}+(b\boldsymbol{i}+c\boldsymbol{j})\epsilon\in\mathbb{DQ}$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $p$ is unitarily equivalent to a dual complex number.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $a=0$, then $p=(b\boldsymbol{i}+c\boldsymbol{j})\epsilon$. By Lemma \ref{1}, the infinitesimal part $b\boldsymbol{i}+c\boldsymbol{j}$ is similar to the complex number $\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}}\boldsymbol{i}\in\mathbb{C}\subseteq\mathbb{DC}$. That is, there is a nonzero quaternion $s$ such that
$$
sps^{-1}=\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon.
$$
In particular, if we take $s$ to have unit norm, then the similarity becomes a unitary equivalence.

If $a\neq 0$, let $u=1+\frac{c\boldsymbol{k}}{2a}\epsilon$ and $v=\frac{u}{|u|}$. Then $v^{\ast}v=vv^{\ast}=1$ and
$$
v^{\ast}pv=v^{\ast}(a\boldsymbol{i})v+v^{\ast}(b\boldsymbol{i}+c\boldsymbol{j})v\epsilon=\frac{a\boldsymbol{i}+b\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon}{|u|^{2}}\in\mathbb{DC}.
$$
Therefore, whether $a$ is zero or not, $p$ is unitarily equivalent to a dual complex number.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{99}
Let $P=P_{st}+P_{\mathcal{I}}\epsilon\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. Then $P$ is unitary in $\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ if and only if $P_{st}$ is unitary $\mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}$ and $P_{st}P_{\mathcal{I}}^{\ast}$ is skew-Hermitian.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{4}
Suppose that $A=A_{st}+A_{\mathcal{I}}\epsilon\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ is a skew-Hermitian matrix. Then there exists a unitary matrix $W\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ and a diagonal matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ such that
$$
\Sigma=WAW^{\ast},
$$
 where
\begin{equation}\label{9}
\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(r_{1}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{11}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,\ldots,r_{1}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{1k_{1}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,r_{2}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{21}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,\ldots,r_{r}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{rk_{r}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon).
\end{equation}
Each diagonal entry of $\Sigma$ is a right eigenvalue of $A$ and
$$
0\leq r_{1}<\cdots<r_{r},\ \  R_{i1}\leq\cdots\leq R_{ik_{i}},\ \ R_{ij}\in\mathbb{R},\ \ \sum_{i=1}^{r}k_{i}=n.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Denote $A=A_{st}+A_{\mathcal{I}}\epsilon\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$, where $A_{st},A_{\mathcal{I}}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}$. Then $A$ is  a skew-Hermitian dual quaternion matrix if and only if both $A_{st}$ and $A_{\mathcal{I}}$ are skew-Hermitian quaternion matrices. It follows from Lemma \ref{264271} that there is a unitary quaternion matrix $U\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}$ and a diagonal matrix $\Lambda$ with the form in (\ref{88}) such that
$$
\Lambda=UA_{st}U^{\ast}.
$$
 Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{1}&=UAU^{\ast}=\Lambda+UA_{\mathcal{I}}U^{\ast}\epsilon\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}
r_{1}I_{k_{1}}\boldsymbol{i}+C_{11}\epsilon & C_{12}\epsilon &  \cdots     &C_{1r}\epsilon  \\
-C_{12}^{\ast}\epsilon  &r_{2}I_{k_{2}}\boldsymbol{i}+C_{22}\epsilon &   \cdots    &  C_{2r}\epsilon\\
 \vdots & \vdots &\ddots & \vdots \\
 -C_{1r}^{\ast}\epsilon & -C_{2r}^{\ast}\epsilon &  \cdots     &r_{r}I_{k_{r}}\boldsymbol{i}+C_{rr}\epsilon
\end{pmatrix},
\end{aligned}
$$
where each $C_{ij}$ is a quaternion matrix of matching dimension and each $C_{ii}$ is a skew-Hermitian quaternion matrix. Let $C_{ij}=M_{ij}+\boldsymbol{j}N_{ij}$, where $M_{ij}$ and $N_{ij}$ are complex matrices with the same dimensions as $C_{ij}$. Define
$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}
P_{11}           &  P_{12} & \cdots & P_{1r}\\
-P_{12}^{\ast}   &  P_{22} & \cdots & P_{2r}\\
\vdots           &  \vdots &\ddots  & \vdots\\
-P_{1r}^{\ast}   &  -P_{2r}^{\ast} &\cdots & P_{rr}
\end{pmatrix},
$$
where for $1\leq s,t\leq r$, each $P_{st}$ is defined as follows,
\begin{enumerate}
\item [(1).]if $s=t$,  $P_{st}=I_{k_{s}}=I_{k_{t}}$;
\item [(2).] if $s<t$,  $P_{st}=\frac{M_{st}}{r_{s}\boldsymbol{i}-r_{t}\boldsymbol{i}}\epsilon+(r_{s}\boldsymbol{i}+r_{t}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\boldsymbol{j}N_{st}\epsilon$;

\item [(3).] if $s>t$,
$P_{st}=-(P_{ts})^{\ast}=
\frac{M_{ts}^{\ast}}{r_{t}\boldsymbol{i}-r_{s}\boldsymbol{i}}\epsilon-N_{ts}^{\ast}\boldsymbol{j}(r_{t}\boldsymbol{i}+r_{s}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\epsilon$.
\end{enumerate}
Since the matrix $P$ is the sum of the identity matrix $I_n$ and a skew-Hermitian matrix, it follows from Lemma \ref{99} that  $P$ is unitary and
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{2}=PA_{1}P^{\ast}&=\mathrm{diag}(r_{1}I_{k_{1}}\boldsymbol{i}+C_{11}\epsilon,\ldots,r_{r}I_{k_{r}}\boldsymbol{i}+C_{rr}\epsilon)\\
&=\mathrm{diag}(r_{1}I_{k_{1}}\boldsymbol{i}+M_{11}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}N_{11}\epsilon,\ldots,r_{r}I_{k_{r}}\boldsymbol{i}+M_{rr}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}N_{rr}\epsilon).
\end{aligned}
$$
Notice that each $M_{ii}$ is a skew-Hermitian complex matrix and each $N_{ii}$ is a symmetric complex matrix by Lemma \ref{264272}. Thus we can find unitary complex matrices $V_{11},\ldots,V_{rr}$ such that each
$$
\Lambda_{ii}=V_{ii}M_{ii}V_{ii}^{\ast}
$$
has the same block form as the matrix $\Lambda$ in Lemma \ref{264271}. That is,
\begin{equation}\label{264282}
\Lambda_{ii}=\mathrm{diag}(\rho_{i1}I_{l_{i1}}\boldsymbol{i},\ldots,\rho_{id_{i}}I_{l_{id_{i}}}\boldsymbol{i}),
\end{equation}
where $\rho_{i1}<\cdots<\rho_{id_{i}},\ l_{i1}+\cdots+l_{id_{i}}=k_{i}$. For each $i$ such that $r_i>0$, set
\[
(R_{i1},\ldots,R_{ik_i})
=
\bigl(
\underbrace{\rho_{i1},\ldots,\rho_{i1}}_{l_{i1}},
\ldots,
\underbrace{\rho_{id_i},\ldots,\rho_{id_i}}_{l_{id_i}}
\bigr).
\]
Denote $V=\mathrm{diag}(V_{11},\ldots,V_{rr})$. Then $V$ is also a unitary complex matrix in $\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ and
$$
A_{3}=VA_{2}V^{\ast}=\mathrm{diag}(r_{1}I_{k_{1}}\boldsymbol{i}+\Lambda_{11}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}E^{11}\epsilon,\ldots,r_{r}I_{k_{r}}\boldsymbol{i}+\Lambda_{rr}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}E^{rr}\epsilon)
$$
is also skew-Hermitian. Therefore, each $E^{ii}$ is symmetric complex. We partition the matrix $E^{ii}$ according to the same block form as matrix $\Lambda_{ii}$ in (\ref{264282}). That is,

\begin{equation}\label{tt}
E^{ii}=\begin{pmatrix}
 E^{ii}_{11}&            E^{ii}_{12} &  \cdots     & E^{ii}_{1d_{i}}  \\
(E^{ii}_{12})^{T}&         E^{ii}_{22} &  \cdots     & E^{ii}_{2d_{i}}   \\
 \vdots        &         \vdots      &  \ddots     & \vdots        \\
(E^{ii}_{1d_{i}})^{T} &       (E^{ii}_{2d_{i}})^{T} &  \cdots     & E^{ii}_{d_{i}d_{i}}
\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
where \(E^{ii}_{st}\in\mathbb C^{l_{is}\times l_{it}}\) for
\(1\leq s,t\leq d_i\).


We now focus on block-diagonalizing $A_{3}$ under unitary equivalence, where the block structure follows that of matrix $\Lambda_{ii}$. One thing to note here is that, during the calculation, we consider the following two cases depending on whether $r_{1}$ is zero or not.
\begin{enumerate}
\item [(1).]$r_{1}\neq 0$. For integers $1\leq h\leq r$, let
$$
Q_{h}=\begin{pmatrix}
I_{l_{h1}} &           (2r_{h}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\boldsymbol{j} E^{hh}_{12}\epsilon &  \cdots     & (2r_{h}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\boldsymbol{j} E^{hh}_{1d_{h}}\epsilon  \\
-(E^{hh}_{12})^{\ast}\boldsymbol{j}(2r_{h}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\epsilon&         I_{l_{h2}} &  \cdots     & (2r_{h}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\boldsymbol{j}E^{hh}_{2d_{h}}\epsilon   \\
 \vdots        &         \vdots      &  \ddots     & \vdots        \\
-(E^{hh}_{1d_{h}})^{\ast}\boldsymbol{j}(2r_{h}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\epsilon &       -(E^{hh}_{2d_{h}})^{\ast}\boldsymbol{j}(2r_{h}\boldsymbol{i})^{-1}\epsilon &  \cdots &   I_{l_{hd_{h}}}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
It follows from the form of $Q_h$ and Lemma \ref{99} that each $Q_{h}$ is unitary. Denote
$$
Q=\begin{pmatrix}
 Q_{1}&     &          \\
&         \ddots &         \\
  & &  Q_{r}
\end{pmatrix},
$$
then $Q$ is a unitary matrix in $\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. And furthermore,
$$
A_{4}=QA_{3}Q^{\ast}=\begin{pmatrix}
 D_{1}&     &          \\
&         \ddots &         \\
  & &  D_{r}
\end{pmatrix},
$$
where for $1\leq p\leq r$, the block matrix
$$
D_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}
r_{p}I_{l_{p1}}\boldsymbol{i}+\rho_{p1}I_{l_{p1}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}E^{pp}_{11}\epsilon &     &          \\
&         \ddots &         \\
  & &  r_{p}I_{l_{pd_{p}}}\boldsymbol{i}+\rho_{pd_{p}}I_{l_{pd_{p}}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}E^{pp}_{d_{p}d_{p}}\epsilon
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Clearly, $A_{4}$ is a block diagonal matrix.

\item [(2).]$r_{1}= 0$. 
 For $2\leq h\leq r$, we repeat the process in the
case $r_1\neq0$. Now, the only block that remains to be handled is
the one containing $r_1$. This block becomes
$\Lambda_{11}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}E^{11}\epsilon$.
Notice that $\Lambda_{11}+\boldsymbol{j}E^{11}$ is a skew-Hermitian quaternion
matrix. Then, by Lemma 3.2, there exists a unitary quaternion matrix
$Q_1\in\mathbb{Q}^{k_1\times k_1}$ such that
\[
Q_1(\Lambda_{11}+jE^{11})Q_1^*
   =\operatorname{diag}(y_1\boldsymbol{i},\ldots,y_{k_1}\boldsymbol{i}),
\qquad
0\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_{k_1}.
\]
Together with the matrices $Q_h$, $2\leq h\leq r$, constructed as in
case (1), let
\[
Q=\operatorname{diag}(Q_1,Q_2,\ldots,Q_r).
\]
Then $A_4=QA_3Q^*$ is block diagonal, and its first diagonal block is
\[
D_1=\operatorname{diag}
(y_1\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,\ldots,y_{k_1}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon).
\]
In this case, set
\[
R_{1\ell}=y_\ell,\qquad \ell=1,\ldots,k_1.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Therefore, in either case, we have successfully transformed $A_{3}$ into the block-diagonal matrix $A_{4}$. Now for $A_{4}$, since each $E^{ii}_{qq}$ is symmetric complex, we may find a unitary complex matrix $Z^{i}_{q}\in\mathbb{C}^{l_{iq}\times l_{iq}}$ such that each
$$
\Theta^{i}_{q}=(Z^{i}_{q})^{T}E^{ii}_{qq}Z^{i}_{q}
$$
is nonnegative diagonal by Lemma \ref{264281}.  Here $1\leq i\leq r$ when
$r_1\neq0$, whereas $2\leq i\leq r$ when $r_1=0$.
If $r_1\neq0$, let
\[
Z=\operatorname{diag}
(Z_1^1,\ldots,Z_{d_1}^1,\ldots,
 Z_1^r,\ldots,Z_{d_r}^r).
\]
If $r_1=0$, let
\[
Z=\operatorname{diag}
(I_{k_1},Z_1^2,\ldots,Z_{d_2}^2,\ldots,
 Z_1^r,\ldots,Z_{d_r}^r).
\]
If $r=1$ and $r_1=0$, we simply take $Z=I_{k_1}$. Then $Z$ is a unitary matrix in $\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$. It then follows from Lemma \ref{12} that,
$$
A_{5}=Z^{\ast}A_{4}Z=\begin{pmatrix}
 G_{1}&     &          \\
&         \ddots &         \\
  & &  G_{r}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
If $r_1=0$, the first block is already diagonal:
\[
G_1=D_1
=\operatorname{diag}
(y_1\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,\ldots,y_{k_1}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon).
\]
All the remaining blocks, as well as all the blocks in the case
$r_1\neq0$, have the form
\begin{equation}
G_{t}=\begin{pmatrix}
r_{t}I_{l_{t1}}\boldsymbol{i}+\rho_{t1}I_{l_{t1}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}\Theta^{t}_{1}\epsilon &  &                 \\
     &  \ddots      &              \\
   &  &  &r_{t}I_{l_{td_{t}}}\boldsymbol{i}+\rho_{td_{t}}I_{l_{td_{t}}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}\Theta^{t}_{d_{t}}\epsilon
\end{pmatrix}.
 \end{equation}
Here $2\leq t\leq r$ if $r_1=0$, whereas $1\leq t\leq r$ if $r_1\neq0$.





If we set $X=Z^{\ast}QVPU$, then $X$ is a unitary matrix in $\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ and $A_{5}=XAX^{\ast}$.

So far, we have completed the task of diagonalizing the original matrix $A$ under unitary equivalence. To make the diagonal entries of $A_{5}$ look more orderly, we now proceed with the following discussion. By Lemma \ref{2}, each diagonal element of matrix $A_{5}$ can be unitarily equivalent to a dual complex number. If we place in order along the diagonal all those unitary elements that convert the diagonal entries of $A_{5}$ into dual complex numbers, the resulting matrix is unitary, we denote it by $Y$. Then furthermore,
$$
\Sigma=YA_{5}Y^{\ast}=YXAX^{\ast}Y^{\ast}.
$$
Let $W=YX$. Then $\Sigma=WAW^{\ast}$. Therefore, under unitary equivalence, the matrix $A$ is finally transformed into the desired form.

By Lemma \ref{2}, when $r_i>0$, each diagonal entry
\[
r_i \boldsymbol{i}+\rho_{iq}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon+\boldsymbol{j}\theta\epsilon
\]
is unitarily equivalent to
\[
r_i \boldsymbol{i}+\rho_{iq}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon.
\]
When $r_1=0$, the first block is already
\[
\operatorname{diag}
(R_{11}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,\ldots,R_{1k_1}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon).
\]
Hence $\Sigma$ has exactly the form in (\ref{9}), with
\[
R_{i1}\leq\cdots\leq R_{ik_i}.
\]

Let $\sigma_m$ be the $m$-th diagonal entry of $\Sigma$, and let
$e_m$ be the $m$-th standard basis vector. Since
\[
\Sigma e_m=e_m\sigma_m
\]
and $\Sigma=WAW^*$, we have
\[
A(W^*e_m)=W^*e_m\sigma_m.
\]
Moreover, $W^*e_m$ is appreciable because $W$ is unitary. Therefore,
every diagonal entry $\sigma_m$ of $\Sigma$ is a right eigenvalue of
$A$.

title: Definition
body_md: Assume $\phi\in\mathbb{S}^{3}$ and $A\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. Define the $\phi$-conjugation of $A$ as $\overline{A}^{\phi}=\overline{\phi} A\phi$, and the $\phi$-transpose of $A$ as $A^{*{\phi}}=\overline{A^*}^{\phi}$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{14}
Assume $\phi\in \mathbb{S}^{3}$,  $A, B\in \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. Then the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}

    \item  $(\overline{A}^{\phi})^* = \overline{A^*}^{\phi}=A^{*{\phi}}$, $(A^{*{\phi}})^{*}=(A^*)^{*{\phi}}$.

    \item If $A$ is invertible, then $(\overline{A}^{\phi})^{-1}=\overline{A^{-1}}^{\phi}$, $(A^{*{\phi}})^{-1}=(A^{-1})^{*{\phi}}$.

    \item $\overline{A+B}^{\phi}=\overline{A}^{\phi}+\overline{B}^{\phi}$, $(A+B)^{*{\phi}}=A^{*{\phi}}+B^{*{\phi}}$.
    \item $\overline{AB}^{\phi}=\overline{A}^{\phi}\cdot\overline{B}^{\phi}$,  $(AB)^{*{\phi}}= B^{*{\phi}}A^{*{\phi}}$.

\item $\overline{A^T}^{\phi}=(\overline{A}^{\phi})^T=\overline{A^{*{\phi}}}=(\overline{A})^{*{\phi}}$.

\item $(A^{*{\phi}})^{T}=(A^{T})^{*{\phi}}=\overline{\overline{A}^{\phi}}=\overline{\overline{A}}^{\phi}  $.
\end{enumerate}

In particular, if $\phi\in \mathbb{S}$ and $A, B\in \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$, then the following equations also hold,
$$
\overline{\overline{A}^{\phi}}^{\phi}=A=(A^{*{\phi}})^{*{\phi}}, \  \overline{A^{*{\phi}}}^{\phi}=(\overline{A}^{\phi})^{*{\phi}}=A^{*}.
$$
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Assume $\phi\in\mathbb{S}^{3}$ and $A\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. If ${\overline{A}^{\phi}}=A^{\ast}$, then we say $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian.
head: environment

label: hh
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{hh}
Generally speaking, when $\phi\in \mathbb{S}^{\prime}$, the equation $\overline{\overline{A}^{\phi}}^{\phi}=A$ does not hold for most $A\in \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. Fortunately,  the equation $A=A^{*{\phi}}(A=-A^{*{\phi}})$ is always equivalent to the equation $\overline{A}^{\phi}=A^{*}(\overline{A}^{\phi}=-A^{*})$. A similar situation also occurs in the preprint \cite{YHX}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Assume $\phi\in\mathbb{S}^{3}$ and $A,B\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. If there exists a unitary matrix $U\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ such that $UAU^{*{\phi}}=B$, then we say $A$ is unitarily $\phi$-congruent to $B$ and denote by $A\sim_{\phi-u} B$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{16}
Suppose that $A=A_{st}+A_{\mathcal{I}}\epsilon\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ is Hermitian. Then there exists a unitary matrix $V\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ and a diagonal matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ such that
$$
\Sigma=V^{\ast}AV,
$$
where
\begin{equation}\label{17}
\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{11}\epsilon,\ldots,\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{1k_{1}}\epsilon,\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{21}\epsilon,\ldots,\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{rk_{r}}\epsilon)
\end{equation}
with the diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ being $n$ eigenvalues of $A$. $\lambda_{i}$ is a $k_{i}$-multiple right eigenvalue of $A_{st}$, and
$$
\lambda_{1}<\cdots<\lambda_{r},\ \  \lambda_{i1}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{ik_{i}},\ \ \lambda_{ij}\in\mathbb{R},\ \ \sum_{i=1}^{r}k_{i}=n.
$$
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{4.1}
Assume $\phi=\pm 1$ and $A\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. If $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian, then there exists a unitary matrix $V\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ and a diagonal matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ such that
$$
\Sigma=VAV^{\ast\phi},
$$
where
\begin{equation}\label{177}
\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{11}\epsilon,\ldots,\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{1k_{1}}\epsilon,\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{21}\epsilon,\ldots,\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{rk_{r}}\epsilon),
\end{equation}
$$
\lambda_{1}<\cdots<\lambda_{r},\ \  \lambda_{i1}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{ik_{i}},\ \ \lambda_{ij}\in\mathbb{R},\ \ \sum_{i=1}^{r}k_{i}=n.
$$
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{3}
Assume $\phi\in\mathbb{S}$ and $A\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. Then $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian if and only if $\phi A$ is skew-Hermitian.
head: environment

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $B$ is $\phi$-Hermitian. This is equivalent to the fact that $\phi B$ is skew-Hermitian by Lemma \ref{3}. Then we can find a unitary matrix $X\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ such that
$$
X(\phi B)X^{\ast}=\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(r_{1}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{11}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,\ldots,r_{1}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{1m_{1}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,r_{2}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{21}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon,\ldots,r_{r}\boldsymbol{i}+R_{rm_{r}}\boldsymbol{i}\epsilon),
$$
where 
$$
0\leq r_{1}<\cdots<r_{r},\ \ R_{i1}\leq\cdots\leq R_{im_{i}},\ \ R_{ij}\in\mathbb{R},\ \ \sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}=n.
$$
By Lemma \ref{1}, $\boldsymbol{i}$ and $\phi$ are unitarily equivalent. Therefore, the diagonal matrix $\Sigma$ can be transformed into
$$
\Xi=\mathrm{diag}(r_{1}\phi+R_{11}\phi\epsilon,\ldots,r_{1}\phi+R_{1m_{1}}\phi\epsilon,r_{2}\phi+R_{21}\phi\epsilon,\ldots,r_{r}\phi+R_{rm_{r}}\phi\epsilon)
$$
through a unitary transformation. We may denote this process by $Y\Sigma Y^{\ast}=\Xi$, where $Y$ is unitary. Now we have
$$
YX(\phi B)X^{\ast}Y^{\ast}=\Xi,
$$
which is equivalent to
$$
\overline{(YX)}^{\phi}B(YX)^{\ast}=\overline{\phi}YX\phi BX^{\ast}Y^{\ast}=\overline{\phi}\Xi.
$$
Denote $\Gamma=\overline{\phi}\Xi$, then $\Gamma$ possesses the desired form in (\ref{13}). By Lemma \ref{14}, we may write $V=\overline{(YX)}^{\phi}$. Then $\overline{V}^{\phi}=YX$ and furthermore $V^{*{\phi}}=(YX)^{\ast}$. Thus, finally
$$
\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ VBV^{*{\phi}}=\Gamma.\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \qedhere
$$
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Assume $\phi\in \mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{R}$. Let $\phi=\phi_{0}+r_{\phi}I_{\phi}$, where 
$$
  r_{\phi}=|\rm{Im}\phi|>0,\ \  I_{\phi}=\frac{Im\phi}{|Im\phi|}  . 
$$  
  Define the set $\mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}$ to be
 $$
 \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}=\{ a+bI_{\phi};a,b\in\mathbb{R}\}.
 $$
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{15}
Let $\phi\in \mathbb{S}^{\prime}$, $A\in \mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}$. If $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian, then $A\in \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}$.
head: environment

label: wa
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{wa}
Let $\phi\in \mathbb{S}^{\prime}$, $A\in \mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}$. If $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian, then $A$ is a Hermitian matrix in $\mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{66}
Let $\phi\in \mathbb{S}^{\prime}$, $A\in \mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}$. If $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian, then there exists a unitary matrix $U\in \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}$ and a real diagonal matrix $\Delta$ such that
$$
\Delta=UA U^{\ast\phi}.
$$
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{55}
Let $\phi\in \mathbb{S}^{\prime}$, $A\in \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. If $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian, then there exists a unitary matrix $W\in \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ and a diagonal matrix $\Lambda$ with dual numbers as its diagonal entries such that
\begin{equation}\label{144}
\Lambda=WA W^{\ast\phi}=\mathrm{diag}\bigl(
r_1+R_{11}\epsilon,\ldots,r_1+R_{1m_1}\epsilon,
r_2+R_{21}\epsilon,\ldots,
r_r+R_{rm_r}\epsilon
\bigr),
\end{equation}
where
\[
r_1<\cdots<r_r,\ \ R_{i1}\leq\cdots\leq R_{im_i},\ \ r_i,R_{ij}\in\mathbb{R},\ \ \sum_{i=1}^{r}m_i=n.
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that for a matrix $A=A_{st}+A_{\mathcal{I}}\epsilon\in\mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$, $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian if and only if both $A_{st}$ and $A_{\mathcal{I}}$ are $\phi$-Hermitian. Then both $A_{st}$ and $A_{\mathcal{I}}$ are in the set $\mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}$ by Lemma \ref{15}. Therefore,
$$
A=A_{st}+A_{\mathcal{I}}\epsilon\in \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}+ \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}\epsilon,
$$
where
$$
\mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}+ \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}\epsilon\cong \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}+ \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\epsilon=\mathbb{DC}^{n\times n}\subseteq \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}.
 $$
 Hence $A$ is a Hermitian matrix in $\mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}+ \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}\epsilon$ by Lemma \ref{wa}. Following from the construction of the unitary matrix in the proof of Lemma \ref{16} (\cite[Theorem 4.1]{QL}), if we replace every $\mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}$ in that process by $\mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}$, then we obtain that there exists a unitary matrix $W\in \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}+ \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}\epsilon \subseteq \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$
such that
$$
WAW^{\ast}=\Lambda,
 $$
 where $\Lambda$ is a diagonal matrix and all the diagonal entries of $\Lambda$ are dual numbers. Furthermore, by $W\in \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}+ \mathbb{C}_{I_{\phi}}^{n\times n}\epsilon$, we have
$$
\Lambda=WAW^{\ast}=WAW^{\ast}\overline{\phi}\phi=WA\overline{\phi}W^{\ast}\phi=WAW^{\ast\phi}.
$$
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\phi\in\mathbb{S}^{3}$, $A\in \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$. If $A$ is $\phi$-Hermitian, then there exists a unitary matrix $W\in \mathbb{DQ}^{n\times n}$ and a diagonal matrix $\Lambda$ with dual numbers as its diagonal entries such that
$$
\Lambda=WA W^{\ast\phi}.
$$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: One should note that regardless of whether the real part of $\phi$ in $\mathbb{S}^{3}$ is zero, the $\phi$-Hermitian dual quaternion matrix $A$ can always be diagonalized to a dual real matrix $\Lambda$ in the sense of unitary $\phi$-congruence. However, when $\phi\in\mathbb{S}$ , the diagonal entries can be nonnegative, whereas when $\phi\in\mathbb{S}^{3}\setminus \mathbb{S}$, they can only be made real.
